frozen_original.title: Trump's All-Out War on the Press: $32M in Forced Settlements, 215 Attack Posts, and a Media Offenders Blacklist
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump's second term saw his long-running enemy of the people rhetoric against journalism convert into systematic, government-backed suppression of the free press at a scale unprecedented in American history. The Freedom of the Press Foundation documented 215 anti-media posts by Trump on Truth Social in 2025, and Poynter's Press Freedom Watch recorded 76 distinct federal actions against journalists during the year. Media companies were coerced into paying $32 million in settlements: ABC paid $15 million toward Trump's presidential library to drop a defamation suit over George Stephanopoulos's on-air statement that Trump was found liable for sexual abuse, and Paramount paid $16 million to settle Trump's lawsuit over 60 Minutes editing — with critics noting Paramount was simultaneously seeking government approval for a Skydance merger, creating an explicit coercion dynamic. On November 28, 2025, the White House launched a media bias tracker on its official website naming and shaming outlets as misleading, biased, exposed, listing the Boston Globe, CBS News, and the Independent as media offenders of the week. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr opened eight investigations into NPR, PBS, ABC, NBC, and CBS; Congress voted in July 2025 to cancel $1.1 billion in subsidies for NPR and PBS. Independent journalist Mario Guevara, who had a valid U.S. work permit, was arrested while covering immigration protests in Atlanta, held for 110 days in conditions he described as including 22-hour daily solitary confinement, then deported to El Salvador — a country he had fled due to death threats — despite his charges being dropped.

children.title: Paramount Settles Trump’s 60 Minutes Lawsuit for $16 Million
children.description_short: Paramount agreed to pay $16 million to settle Trump’s lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview; the settlement did not establish that the interview was improperly edited.
children.description_medium: On July 2, 2025, Paramount agreed to pay $16 million to settle Donald Trump’s lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. PBS NewsHour reported that Trump alleged the interview was edited to improve how Harris sounded, which CBS denied. Paramount said the money would go to Trump’s future presidential library and that CBS would not issue an apology. PBS also reported that Paramount was seeking merger approval from the Trump administration; concerns about a connection were reported as allegations, not proven as an exchange.
children.description_long: On July 2, 2025, Paramount agreed to pay Donald Trump $16 million to settle his lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump alleged that the interview had been edited to improve how Harris sounded; CBS denied the allegation. Paramount said the payment would go to the president’s future library and that the settlement did not require an apology. The case therefore ended in a payment, not a court finding that CBS had manipulated the interview. PBS NewsHour’s report also described a separate context: Paramount was seeking administration approval for its proposed Skydance merger, and interview guest Brian Stelter said that was why the word “bribe” had come up in public discussion. Paramount and the FCC denied that suggestion. The reporting does not establish that merger review was exchanged for the settlement or that the administration conditioned approval on payment. This entry records the settlement and the attributed concern without treating coercion as a proven fact. Other incidents in the original card are handled separately.

children.description_short: Trump signed a rescission bill that canceled about $1.1 billion allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, according to AP reporting published by PBS.
children.description_medium: On July 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a bill canceling about $9 billion in previously approved foreign-aid and public-broadcasting spending. The Associated Press, published by PBS NewsHour, said about $1.1 billion was allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which finances NPR and PBS, with most of that amount distributed to more than 1,500 local stations. children.description_long: On July 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a rescission bill that canceled about $9 billion in previously approved spending for public broadcasting and foreign aid. The Associated Press reported through PBS NewsHour that about $1.1 billion had been allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which financed NPR and PBS; most of that amount was distributed to more than 1,500 local public radio and television stations. The article describes a completed federal rescission, not merely a proposed cut. It says the White House had presented the bill as a test case for additional rescission packages and reports that Democrats unanimously opposed it but could not stop it. This card is limited to the signed rescission and the reported funding channel. It does not claim that the entire $1.1 billion would have gone directly to NPR or PBS, that every local station lost the same amount, or that specific station closures followed. The original record grouped this measure with separate legal disputes, media criticism, FCC inquiries, and immigration enforcement; those actions are not part of this dated entry.

frozen_original.title: Trump Cuts All US Aid to Palestinians
frozen_original.synopsis: In 2025, the Trump administration completed a comprehensive severance of all US humanitarian and development aid to Palestinians, building on the UNRWA funding cuts from the first term. The cuts affected USAID programs supporting healthcare, water sanitation, economic development, and governance in the West Bank, in addition to the continued ban on UNRWA funding. The complete elimination of Palestinian aid — totaling hundreds of millions of dollars annually — was justified by administration officials as pressure on the Palestinian Authority and Hamas, but aid organizations warned the cuts would accelerate a humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza where malnutrition and disease were already at crisis levels. The cuts violated US legal obligations under the Foreign Assistance Act which require humanitarian aid to be provided regardless of political disputes.

primary.title: Trump’s Foreign Aid Freeze Disrupts Gaza Assistance Despite Exemptions
primary.description_short: Trump’s Foreign Aid Freeze Disrupts Gaza Assistance Despite Exemptions
primary.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump ordered a 90-day pause on foreign aid while programs were reviewed. Reuters reported that exemptions included $78 million for non-food humanitarian assistance in Gaza, while the Associated Press later reported that hundreds of millions in USAID payments to aid groups remained frozen and officials had no confirmed payments to Middle East partners. The evidence supports disruption, not a complete cutoff of all Palestinian aid.
primary.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump ordered a 90-day pause on foreign aid while the administration reviewed whether programs aligned with its foreign-policy priorities. Reuters reported that the pause halted funding across assistance programs and later reviewed a list of exemptions, finding that only limited humanitarian relief was released. Among the approved exceptions were $78 million for non-food humanitarian assistance in Gaza. That limited carveout makes the frozen entry’s claim that all U.S. aid to Palestinians was eliminated inaccurate. The interruption still had reported effects: in March, the Associated Press reported that hundreds of millions of dollars in USAID contractual payments to aid groups were frozen, and that officials had no confirmed payments to partners in the Middle East after the January 31 Gaza waiver. The reporting distinguishes authorization from delivery: more than $383 million was approved for Gaza relief, while payment remained unconfirmed. The supported event is therefore a broad aid freeze that disrupted Gaza assistance despite exceptions, not a completed categorical cutoff of every Palestinian program. The cited reports do not establish the frozen entry’s annual aid total, a Foreign Assistance Act violation, or a specific administration rationale about Palestinians.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump’s Foreign Aid Freeze Disrupts Gaza Assistance Despite Exemptions
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump’s Foreign Aid Freeze Disrupts Gaza Assistance Despite Exemptions
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump ordered a 90-day pause on foreign aid while programs were reviewed. Reuters reported that exemptions included $78 million for non-food humanitarian assistance in Gaza, while the Associated Press later reported that hundreds of millions in USAID payments to aid groups remained frozen and officials had no confirmed payments to Middle East partners. The evidence supports disruption, not a complete cutoff of all Palestinian aid.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump ordered a 90-day pause on foreign aid while the administration reviewed whether programs aligned with its foreign-policy priorities. Reuters reported that the pause halted funding across assistance programs and later reviewed a list of exemptions, finding that only limited humanitarian relief was released. Among the approved exceptions were $78 million for non-food humanitarian assistance in Gaza. That limited carveout makes the frozen entry’s claim that all U.S. aid to Palestinians was eliminated inaccurate. The interruption still had reported effects: in March, the Associated Press reported that hundreds of millions of dollars in USAID contractual payments to aid groups were frozen, and that officials had no confirmed payments to partners in the Middle East after the January 31 Gaza waiver. The reporting distinguishes authorization from delivery: more than $383 million was approved for Gaza relief, while payment remained unconfirmed. The supported event is therefore a broad aid freeze that disrupted Gaza assistance despite exceptions, not a completed categorical cutoff of every Palestinian program. The cited reports do not establish the frozen entry’s annual aid total, a Foreign Assistance Act violation, or a specific administration rationale about Palestinians.

frozen_original.synopsis: On March 18, 2025, President Trump posted on Truth Social and repeated in press statements the sweeping claim that no federal court had the authority to stop him from deporting individuals under what he described as the President's inherent constitutional power over foreign nationals and national security — a claim advanced in the context of ongoing court orders blocking Alien Enemies Act deportations. The declaration went beyond any recognized legal theory, asserting that immigration enforcement was categorically exempt from judicial review regardless of constitutional violations, treaty obligations, or statutory requirements. Legal scholars from across the political spectrum — including prominent conservative constitutional lawyers — categorically rejected the claim as incompatible with Article III of the Constitution and two centuries of judicial precedent. The statement was accompanied by Trump's announcement that he considered himself personally immune from contempt proceedings, completing his articulation of a theory of absolute presidential immunity from all legal accountability.
